texts.preamble: Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Author: P.Sam Koshy Bench: P.Sam Koshy, N.Tukaramji The Hon'Ble Sri Justice P.Sam Koshy And The Hon'Ble Sri Justice N.Tukaramji Writ Pettion No.25901 of 2024 Order:
texts.facts: 2. The instant is a writ petition which has been filed challenging the order dated 03.01.2022 (Annexure P-1) passed by respondent No.2 putting detenu under preventive detention under Sub-Section (2) of Section 3 of the "The Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities of Bootleggers, Dacoits, Drug-Offenders, Goondas, Immoral Traffic Offenders, Land-Grabbers, Spurious Seed Offenders, Insecticide Offenders, Fertiliser Offenders, Food Adulteration Offenders, Fake Document Offenders, Scheduled Commodities Offenders, Forest Offenders, Gaming Offenders, Sexual Offenders, Explosive Substances Offenders, Arms Offenders, Cyber Crime Offenders and White Collar or Financial Offenders Act, 1986 (for short, 'the Act of 1986'). 3. The writ petition is one which has been filed seeking for issuance of a Writ in the nature of Habeas Corpus with prayer for production of the detenu before the Court and quashment of the aforementioned orders. 4. The facts of the case in brief are that the detenu has committed an offence under Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act, 1986 across various Police Station limits where detenu was involved in NDPS Act engaged in illegal and highly dangerous activities of peddling Contraband Cannabis / Ganja among the innocents which was registered within the jurisdiction of Hyderabad and Cyberabad Police Commissionerate indicating a pattern of persistent and organized drug trafficking. On 25.10.2021, the police authorities had apprehended the detenu near St. Anns College Lane, Mehdipatnam, in connection with the possession and peddling of 'Ganja' (marijuana), a narcotic substance prohibited under NDPS Act. Upon arrest, the police authorities seized 1120 grams of Ganja packed in 28 covers of 40 grams each, a Jio cell phone, a Honda Destini scooter without number plate and Rs.2,000/- in cash. The seizure was conducted under a confession-cum-seizure panchanama and samples were sent to the Telangana State Forensic Science Laboratories (TSFSL) in Red Hills, Hyderabad, which confirmed the substance as 'Ganja'. The detenu was charged under Case No.243/2021, Section 8(c) read with Section 20(b) of the NDPS Act, and was subsequently remanded to judicial custody. Previously, the detenu was arrested in four Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/38511165/ 1 cases related to Ganja peddling offenses in Hyderabad and one in Cyberabad establishing a pattern of habitual drug related activities. Despite being granted conditional bail in previous cases, the authority concerned believed that he is likely continue his illegal activities. The authority concerned expressed grave concern over the impact of detenu's actions involved in procuring Ganja from undisclosed sources and selling it to the innocent people especially youth; for easy money, posing significant threat to society and also causing irreparable damages to their central nervous system and thereby crippling the mental and physical health of the people. Due to the severity and repetitive nature of the offence, the authority concerned passed the preventive detention order on 03.01.2022 and classified detenu as "Drug-Offender". 5. Thus, the impugned order was under challenged on the grounds that these alleged crimes fall under the purview of ordinary law and do not constitute a disturbance of public order, questioning the necessity and legality of the detention order under the Telangana Prevention of Dangerous Activities Act.
texts.arguments: 6. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that a plain reading of the impugned order would reveal that the detention order against the detenu is unconstitutional and illegal. He argued that the detention order does not warrant invocation of preventive detention laws and that the detaining authority failed to differentiate between acts affecting law and order and those affecting public order. Further, the learned counsel for the petitioner contended that the authority concerned did not consider the detenu's compliance with bail conditions and his lack of involvement in other cases since release. Furthermore, the learned counsel for the petitioner contended that detention order has passed mechanically without proper application of mind and based on flimsy grounds. 7. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that there is insufficient material to justify treating the detenu as a drug offender under the Act of 1986 and that the cases mentioned can be dealt with under ordinary law. Additionally, the detaining authority allegedly failed to consider the conditional bail granted in four cases, which already placed the detenu under police surveillance making preventive detention unnecessary. Further, it was argued that there is lack of prima facie evidence against the detenu in the registered cases and the complaints are vague and also intended to harass him. Moreover, respondent No.2 did not follow the mandatory procedure before invoking the provisions of Sub-Section (2) of Section 3 of the Act of 1986 rendering the detention order liable to [LEAKAGE_MASK]. 8. Per contra, the learned Special Government Pleader argued that the detenu is a habitual drug offender and his involvement in multiple cases of Ganja peddling within the Hyderabad Police Commissionerate and one in Cyberabad. Moreover, there are multiple cases registered against the detenu including Cr.No.11 of 2021 at Shahinayathgunj Police Station, Cr.No.18 of 2021 at Shahinayathgunj Police Station, Cr.No.124 of 2021 at Prohibition and Excise Station, Dhoolpet, Cr.No.243 of 2021 of Asifnagar Police Station and Cr.No.849 of 2018 at Mailardevpally Police Station, Cyberabad. All these cases clearly demonstrate that the detenu's ongoing engagement in drug trafficking, despite previous arrest and legal action, the detenu continued his engagement in illegal activities, particularly the peddling of Ganja which shows a pattern of behavior that poses an ongoing threat to public order and health. Furthermore, he argued that the ripple effects of drug Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/38511165/ 2 addiction extended beyond the immediate users, impacting family dynamics, educational outcomes, and overall community well- being. 9. Learned Special Government Pleader further argued that the prolonged nature of Court proceedings could potentially allow detenu to continue harming society while out on bail and also poses risk at large in the view of repeated offences. It was also argued that this preventive detention is not merely punitive, but serves a crucial preventive function aimed at breaking the cycle of drug peddling and its associated crime. Thus, removing detenu from society, ensuring a balance between public safety and individual rights demonstrate a comprehensive approach to combat drug related crimes while maintain due process of law. In the said judgment, the Hon'ble Supreme Court in paragraph Nos.23, 24 and 25 dealing with the explanation attached to Section 2(a) has held as under, viz., "23. The explanation attached to Section 2(a) of the Act 1986 reproduced above contemplates that 'public order' shall be deemed to have been affected adversely or shall be deemed likely to be affected adversely, inter alia if any of the activities of any person referred to in Section 2(a) directly or indirectly, are causing or is likely to cause any harm, danger or alarm or feeling of insecurity among the general public or any section thereof or a grave or widespread danger to life, property or public health. The Explanation to Section 2(a) also provides that for the purpose of Section 2, a person shall be deemed to be "acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order" when such person is a "GOONDA" and engaged in activities which affect adversely or are likely to affect adversely the maintenance of public order. Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/38511165/ 3 24. The essential concept of preventive detention is that the detention of a person is not to punish him for something he has done but to prevent him from doing it. A criminal conviction on the other hand is for an act already done which can only be possible by a trial and legal evidence. One is a punitive action and the other is a preventive act. The power of preventive detention is a precautionary power exercised in reasonable anticipation. (See :HaradhanSaha v. The State of W.B., 1974 Cri LJ 1479]" 12. Again in paragraph No.32, the Hon'ble Supreme Court has in great detail dealt with the expression 'law and order' and 'public order' and held as under, viz., "32. The crucial issue is whether the activities of the detenu were prejudicial to public order. While the expression 'law and order' is wider in scope inasmuch as contravention of law always affects order, 'Public order' has a narrower ambit, and could be affected by only such contravention, which affects the community or the public at large. Public order is the even tempo of life of the community taking the country as a whole or even a specified locality. The distinction between the areas of 'law and order' and 'public order' is one of degree and extent of the reach, of the act in question on society. It is the potentiality of the act to disturb the even tempo of life of the community which makes it prejudicial to the maintenance of the public order. In other words, the true distinction between the areas of law and order and public order lies not merely in the nature or quality of the act, but in the degree and extent of its reach upon society. In one case it might affect specific individuals only, and therefore touches the problem of law and order only, while in another it might affect public order. In its quality it may not differ from other similar acts, but in its potentiality, that is, in its impact on society, it may be very different. [See: Union of India v. Amrit Lal Manchanda, (2004) 3 SCC 75.]" Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/38511165/ 4 13. In yet another land mark decision in Ameena Begum vs. The State of Telangana 9, a judgment which has been pronounced under the same provision of law, the Hon'ble Supreme Court held at paragraph Nos.34 to 37 as under: (2023) 9 SCC 587 "34. In Kuso Sah vs. The State of Bihar, Hon'ble Y.V. Chandrachud, J. (as the Chief Justice then was) speaking for the Bench held that: "4.*** The two concepts have well defined contours, it being well established that stray and un-organised crimes of theft and assault are not matters of public order since they do not tend to affect the even flow of public life. Infractions of law are bound in some measure to lead to disorder but every infraction of law does not necessarily result in public disorder. ** * 6. *** The power to detain a person without the safeguard of a court trial is too drastic to permit a lenient construction and therefore Courts must be astute to ensure that the detaining authority does not transgress the limitations subject to which alone the power can be exercised. ** *" (underlining ours, for emphasis) 35. Turning our attention to section 3(1) of the Act, the Government has to arrive at a subjective satisfaction that a goonda (as in the present case) has to be detained, in order to prevent him from acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. "Public order" is defined in the Explanation to section 2(a) of the Act as encompassing situations that cause "harm, danger or alarm or a feeling of insecurity among the general public or any section thereof or a grave wide-spread danger to life or public health". 36. Ram Manohar Lohia (supra) is an authority to rely upon for the proposition that if liberty of an individual can be invaded under statutory rules by the simple process of making of a certain order, he can be so deprived only if the order is in consonance with the said rule. Strict compliance with the letter of the rule, in such a case, has to be the essence of the matter since the statute has the potentiality to interfere with the personal liberty of an individual and a Court is precluded from going behind its face. If there is any doubt whether the rules have been strictly observed, that doubt must be resolved in favour of the detenu. It is said in paragraph 30 that: Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/38511165/ 5 "30. Whenever an order under a preventive detention law is challenged one of the questions the court must ask in deciding its legality is: was the ordinary law of the land sufficient to deal with the situation? 14. This Bench observed that there is an adequate distinction between acts affecting public order and those merely related to law and order, where this distinction was emphasized by the Apex Court in Nenavath Bujji (supra). This detention order does not conclusively demonstrate how the detenu's drug related activities had widespread impact on society rather than being confined to specific individuals or instances. 15. Despite the directives from the Hon'ble Supreme Court and this Court, it is unfortunate that preventive detention continues to be routinely employed by authorities in Telangana. The Court has repeatedly noted that authorities often struggle to differentiate between actions that disrupt law and order and those that genuinely threaten public order. As elucidated in the Supreme Court judgments of Nenavath Bujji (supra) and Ameena Begum (supra) public order refers to the "even tempo of life of the community" and has significantly narrower ambit than 'law and order'. 16. This distinction is crucial in maintaining the delicate balance between societal protection and individual rights that forms the bedrock of our democratic legal system. This scenario was resonate with the Rekha case, which unequivocally stated that if the ordinary law of the land is sufficient to deal Thakur Jyothi vs The State Of Telangana on 30 October, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/38511165/ 6 with the situation a detention order becomes illegal.
